books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, A. Slave Rebellions

stimulus.text:
Gabriel: In 1800, Gabriel, an enslaved blacksmith in Richmond, Virginia, planned a rising with as many as a thousand men, hoping to win freedom and a republican government. A heavy rainstorm delayed the march, two enslaved men warned their owners, and the militia stopped the rising before it began. Gabriel and 25 others were hanged.

Denmark Vesey: In 1822, Denmark Vesey, a free Black carpenter in Charleston, South Carolina, and a leader in the city’s Black Methodist church, was tried for plotting a rising. He and others were hanged. The main evidence against him came from testimony in court by accused men facing punishment themselves, so historians still argue about whether a plot existed at all.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 A. Slave Rebellions, including the sourcing box on the Denmark Vesey conspiracy.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 A
stem: Gabriel’s plan drew on the republican ideas debated by Virginia Democratic-Republicans in the 1790s. That connection best shows that

options.text: enslaved people followed American political debates and used them to claim freedom
Virginia’s Democratic-Republicans had planned the rising with Gabriel
options.misconception: Gabriel adopted their ideas; no partnership with them is shown.

options.text: Gabriel hoped the federal government would send troops to free him
options.misconception: Gabriel planned his own rising, not a rescue by federal troops.

options.text: most Virginia planters supported Gabriel’s republican ideas
options.misconception: The militia stopped him and planters hanged him.

rationales.A: Gabriel heard republican talk in Richmond and framed his rising as a republican revolution. He turned American ideas against slavery.
rationales.B: No partnership is shown. Gabriel adopted the ideas of Virginia Democratic-Republicans; they did not plan with him.
rationales.C: Gabriel recruited a thousand men for his own rising. He did not wait for federal troops.
rationales.D: Planters did not support him. The militia stopped the rising, and Gabriel was hanged.
rationales.general:
1. Note where Gabriel worked. As a hired-out blacksmith in Richmond he met artisans and heard political talk.
2. Note what he took from it. He framed his rising as a republican revolution, not only as revenge.
3. Name the point. Enslaved people were not cut off from American ideas; they turned those ideas against slavery.
Background: Gabriel was trained as a blacksmith and frequently hired out to Richmond employers.
Remember: ideas travel through work and talk, and people shut out of power can still pick them up.
